newsitem.title: USA: Lucent to offer faster modem chip by '97 Q1.
newsitem.headline: Lucent to offer faster modem chip by '97 Q1.

text.p: Lucent Technologies Inc joined the race to offer modem products capable of running at nearly twice the speed of current modems operating over conventional copper wire phone lines.

Lucent's Microelectronics Group division said Wednesday it had developed computer chip technology to allow PC users to access the Internet at speeds of up to 56 kilobits per second, nearly double the current 28.8 standard.
It said it would begin shipping its first digital signal processing chip based on the 56 kilobit technology by the first quarter of 1997.

Lucent said its chips are based on V.flex 2 technology developed at Bell Laboratories, the research and development arm of Lucent, which has patented key elements of the new 56 kilobit technology and has other required patents pending.
The company said it is working with leading Internet service equipment providers to ensure maximum interoperability for customers of 56 kilobit technology.
Lucent said the first two chips to incorporate the new technology are the DSP1643 and the DSP1674. It plans to incorporate the technology into other chips as well.

Earlier today, U.S. Robotics Corp confirmed it had developed a new modem running at up to 56 kilobit speeds, which it plans to begin field testing in November and introduce in the first quarter of 1997.
U.S. Robotics is the leading maker of standalone consumer modem products.

U.S. Robotics's stock has soared in recent weeks on speculation it was about to introduce the new technology, which would help address a key constraint on Internet communications over the existing phone network.

Semiconductor maker Motorola Inc has said it plans to introduce 56 kilobit products in 1997, and Rockwell International Corp's semiconductor unit has said it plans to demonstrate 56 kilobit technology in November.
Rockwell is the world's leading maker of modem chips.
Several modem suppliers have announced plans to offer 56 kilobit modem products based on Rockwell technology, including Ascend Communications Inc and Boca Research Inc.
Lucent's DSP1643 chip is designed for use in personal computers running Microsoft Windows operating systems, Lucent said.
The DSP1674 is for use in Internet and online service providers' server computer equipment.
Lucent said it plans to demonstrate its 56 kilobit technology at the annual COMDEX computer industry trade show in Las Vegas November 18-22.
